items.hint1: This question asks you to match a definition to the name of a value. Pick out the key words in the definition before you look at the options.
items.hint2: The key words are 'training of oneself', 'rules' and 'self-control'. Contentment is about being satisfied with what you have, so it does not match.
items.hint3: Of the values left, which one is about obeying rules and controlling your own behaviour, rather than about honesty or dedication?
items.solution:
Answer: B. discipline

Discipline is the value of training yourself to obey rules and to control your own behaviour, even when nobody is watching you. It is built by habit, so it is described as training.

How to tell: the definition has three clues, 'training of oneself', 'self-rules' and 'self-control'. All three describe discipline.

Why not the others:
A. integrity: this is being honest and holding firmly to good moral principles, not training yourself to obey rules.
C. contentment: this is being satisfied with what you have, not self-control through rules.
D. commitment: this is dedication to a duty, cause or promise, not training in self-control.

Exam tip: in 'which value is this' questions, underline the key words in the definition and match them to one value. Rules and self-control point to discipline, honesty points to integrity, and satisfaction points to contentment.

items.hint1: Each option is a word placed before 'value'. Think about what each word means on its own, then fit it to the definition.
items.hint2: Mobilization means gathering people together for a cause, and classification means sorting things into groups. Neither is about each person working out what they believe.
items.hint3: You are left with two terms. Which one means making something clear, so that a person understands their own values while respecting other people's?
items.solution:
Answer: B. clarification

Value clarification is the process in which each person is helped to find out and state clearly what their own values are, while learning to respect that other people may hold different values. To clarify means to make clear.

How to tell: the definition says people 'define their own values' and 'respect other people's values'. Making your own values clear to yourself is clarification.

Why not the others:
A. mobilization: this means gathering people together for a cause, not each person defining their own values.
C. classification: this means sorting values into groups or types, not a person working out what they believe.
D. orientation: this refers to the general direction of a person's values, or being guided towards a set of values, rather than people defining their own.

Exam tip: for value terms, think about the plain meaning of the word in front. Clarify means make clear, reorient means turn back to a new direction, and classify means sort into groups.

items.hint1: This is about one of the ways a foreigner can become a Nigerian citizen. The Constitution sets conditions for age and for how long the person has lived in Nigeria.
items.hint2: In Nigeria, full age is 18 years. That rules out the options that ask for 21 years.
items.hint3: Both remaining options say 18 years. Now recall how many years a person must have lived in Nigeria before applying: is it 15 or 25?
items.solution:
Answer: A. 18 years old and above and have spent at least 15 years in Nigeria

Naturalisation is the way a foreigner who has lived in Nigeria for a long time can apply to become a citizen. Section 27 of the 1999 Constitution requires the person to be of full age, which the Constitution sets at 18 years, and to have lived in Nigeria for at least 15 years, along with other conditions such as good character.

How to tell: first check the age. Full age is 18, so only A and B remain. Then check the years of residence. The Constitution asks for 15 years, not 25.

Why not the others:
B. 25 years in Nigeria: the age is right, but the residence period is longer than the Constitution requires.
C. 21 years and 10 years: 21 is not the age of full age in the Constitution, and 10 years of residence is too short.
D. 21 years and 5 years: the age is wrong and 5 years of residence is far too short.

Exam tip: for naturalisation questions, remember two numbers together: 18 years of age and 15 years of residence. Check the age first, because it usually cuts the options in half.

items.hint1: Think about what kind of citizen Civic Education is trying to produce.
items.hint2: Studying the physical environment, such as rivers, relief and climate, belongs to Geography, not Civic Education.
items.hint3: Of the options left, one describes a positive goal and the others describe something harmful or half-done. Which one builds love and loyalty for the country?
items.solution:
Answer: B. inculcates the spirit of nationalism and patriotism in the citizens of a state

Civic Education aims to produce good citizens who know their rights and duties, hold good values, and love and serve their country. To inculcate means to plant an idea firmly in someone's mind by teaching it again and again.

How to tell: the major reason must be a positive goal about citizens and the nation. Building nationalism and patriotism is exactly that.

Why not the others:
A. encourages the struggle for political power: Civic Education teaches responsible participation, not a struggle for power.
C. helps them understand their physical environment: that is the work of Geography.
D. identifies problems without offering solutions: Civic Education aims to help citizens solve society's problems, not just point them out.

Exam tip: for 'why study Civic Education' questions, choose the option about producing good, patriotic and responsible citizens. Reject options that are negative or belong to another subject.

items.hint1: A national symbol stands for the whole country. Ask of each option whether it represents Nigeria as a nation.
items.hint2: Things like the flag and coat of arms belong to the nation as a whole and are the same for every citizen.
items.hint3: Which option is a personal document issued to one individual, carrying their own name and photograph?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Voters card

A national symbol is something that represents the whole country and its identity, such as the national flag, the national anthem, the national pledge, the coat of arms and the national currency.

How to tell: a voter's card is issued by INEC to one person so that they can vote. It carries that person's details and identifies them, not the nation. The other three represent Nigeria as a whole.

Why not the others:
A. National flag: it is a national symbol, representing the country with its green and white colours.
C. National currency: the naira is a national symbol, shared by the whole country.
D. Coat of arms: it is a national symbol, used on official documents to represent the country.

Exam tip: in 'which is not a national symbol' questions, look for the item that belongs to one person or one office. Symbols stand for the whole nation.

items.hint1: Think about what the nationalists were fighting against, and how a newspaper could help that fight.
items.hint2: Nationalists wanted to end colonial rule, so their newspapers were aimed at the colonial government, not at protecting chiefs.
items.hint3: Two options are left in play: one is about the colonial government and one is about the nationalists themselves. Which was the main purpose of the papers in the struggle for independence?
items.solution:
Answer: A. revealing the weaknesses of the colonial powers

Nationalist newspapers, such as Nnamdi Azikiwe's West African Pilot and Herbert Macaulay's Lagos Daily News, were used to expose the wrongs and failures of colonial rule. By showing people these weaknesses, they turned public opinion against colonial rule and built support for independence.

How to tell: the nationalists' aim was self-rule. A newspaper helps that aim by exposing the colonial government's failures, which is what textbooks list as the press's contribution.

Why not the others:
B. fighting racial discrimination: the papers did criticise unfair treatment, but textbooks do not list this as their main role.
C. protecting the rights of traditional rulers: many traditional rulers worked with the colonial government under indirect rule, so this was not the papers' purpose.
D. promoting the image of the nationalists: the papers did make their owners well known, but that was a side effect, not their main contribution.

Exam tip: when asked what nationalists or their tools achieved, pick the option that attacks colonial rule or pushes for independence. Options about personal fame are usually side effects.

items.hint1: Start from what nationalism means: a strong feeling of love for and belonging to one's nation.
items.hint2: Human rights awareness is a separate topic in Civic Education and is not the core of nationalism.
items.hint3: Several options sound good. Which one describes the loyalty itself, rather than something that follows from it or helps spread it?
items.solution:
Answer: B. create a sense of allegiance to the nation

Nationalism is a strong feeling of love, loyalty and belonging to one's nation. Its main significance for development is that it makes citizens give their allegiance, meaning loyalty, to the nation, so they work together for it rather than only for their tribe or region.

How to tell: allegiance means loyalty. Loyalty to the nation is the heart of nationalism, and the other benefits grow out of it.

Why not the others:
A. foster a sense of selflessness: selflessness can follow from loyalty to the nation, but it is not the main thing nationalism creates.
C. promote awareness of fundamental human rights: that belongs to the human rights topic, not the core of nationalism.
D. create a sense of political awareness: nationalist movements did raise political awareness, but that was the means by which nationalism spread, not its main significance.

Exam tip: when several options are true effects, choose the one closest to the definition of the term. For nationalism, that is loyalty or allegiance to the nation.

items.hint1: This is a straight recall question about the United Nations document adopted in 1948.
items.hint2: Do not be tricked by the year. The number of articles has nothing to do with 1948.
items.hint3: Set aside any option built from the date, and any above 40. Of the two left, which is the article count you learned?
items.solution:
Answer: A. 30

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December 1948. It sets out the basic rights every human being is entitled to in 30 articles.

How to tell: this is a fact to remember. The UDHR has 30 articles. December 10 is marked each year as Human Rights Day.

Why not the others:
B. 33: this is not the number of articles in the UDHR.
C. 48: this is taken from the year, 1948, to catch students who mix up the date and the number.
D. 50: this is not the number of articles in the UDHR.

Exam tip: for UDHR questions, remember the set of facts: United Nations, 10 December 1948, 30 articles. When an option repeats part of a date, be suspicious of it.

items.hint1: Picture a person inside a prison. Which freedoms are taken away by being locked up?
items.hint2: Each option names two rights, and both must be lost. A prisoner still has the right to life while serving a prison term, so any option with it cannot be fully right.
items.hint3: A prisoner has already had a trial and can still appeal, so fair hearing is not lost. Which option has two rights that are both lost by being kept behind walls?
items.solution:
Answer: C. right to movement and association

When a court convicts a person and sends them to prison, the law takes away the rights that imprisonment itself cannot allow. A prisoner cannot move freely and cannot freely meet or join with other people. Those are the rights to freedom of movement and freedom of association.

How to tell: check both rights in each option. In C, both movement and association are clearly lost behind prison walls. Every other option contains at least one right the prisoner keeps.

Why not the others:
A. freedom of expression and right to fair hearing: a prisoner keeps the right to fair hearing, for example to appeal the conviction.
B. right to life and right to personal liberty: liberty is lost, but a prison sentence does not take away the right to life.
D. right to fair hearing and right to movement: movement is lost, but fair hearing is kept.

Exam tip: when each option pairs two rights, test both. One wrong right makes the whole option wrong.

items.hint1: The key word in the question is 'writes'. Harming someone's good name falls under defamation, which has two forms.
items.hint2: Blackmail is demanding money or favours by threatening someone, and sedition is words that stir up rebellion against the government. Neither is about damaging one person's reputation.
items.hint3: One form of defamation is spoken and the other is written or published. Which one fits a social media post?
items.solution:
Answer: D. libel

Defamation is making a false statement that damages another person's reputation. It has two forms: libel, which is written, printed or published, and slander, which is spoken. Freedom of expression is limited by the rights of other people, so defamation is an offence.

How to tell: the person wrote the false statement and posted it on social media. It is written and published, so it is libel.

Why not the others:
A. blackmail: this is demanding money or favours by threatening a person, not publishing false statements.
B. sedition: this is speech or writing that stirs up hatred or rebellion against the government, not damage to one person's name.
C. slander: this is defamation by spoken words, but here the statement was written.

Exam tip: to tell libel from slander, link libel with literature (written) and slander with speech (spoken).

items.hint1: The question describes one of the principles of the rule of law. Look for the key phrase 'irrespective of their status'.
items.hint2: Fair hearing and the right to appeal are about how a trial is run, not about whether the law covers everyone.
items.hint3: Two principles are left. One says the law is above everyone's power; the other says the law treats every person the same. Which fits 'applies to everyone irrespective of status'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. equality before the law

Equality before the law is the principle of the rule of law that every person, rich or poor, leader or ordinary citizen, is subject to the same laws and treated the same way by the courts.

How to tell: 'irrespective of their status' means no matter how important or unimportant a person is. The law treating all people alike is equality before the law.

Why not the others:
A. supremacy of the law: this means the law is above any person or government and no one may act outside it, not specifically that all persons are treated alike.
B. fair hearing: this means a person must be heard by a fair court before being judged, not that the law covers everyone equally.
D. right to appeal: this is the right to take a case to a higher court, not a statement about equal treatment.

Exam tip: the key words decide rule of law questions. 'irrespective of status' or 'treated alike' points to equality before the law; 'the law is supreme' or 'no arbitrary power' points to supremacy of the law.

items.hint1: Constituted authority is power given by law, such as the government, police and courts. Ask what society would lose without it.
items.hint2: Scholarships and international relations are things a government may do, but they are not the basic reason society needs authority.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, ask which one society would lose first if there were no police, courts or government at all.
items.solution:
Answer: B. ensures security of life and property

Constituted authority is power that is set up and recognised by law, such as the government, police, courts and traditional rulers. Society needs it to make and enforce laws and keep order, and without order no one's life or property would be safe.

How to tell: the question asks why authority is necessary. The most basic reason is maintaining law and order so that lives and property are protected.

Why not the others:
A. promotes international relations: this is one activity of government, not the reason authority is needed in society.
C. serves as an agent of socialization: agents of socialization are the family, school, peers and media, which teach people how to live in society.
D. provides scholarship for higher education: this is a service some governments give, not the basic purpose of authority.

Exam tip: when asked why authority, government or law is needed, look for law and order or security of life and property. Services such as scholarships are extras.

items.hint1: Think about what responsible parents give their children, and how that shows up in society.
items.hint2: Responsible parenthood is about raising well-behaved children, not specifically about politics or making leaders strict.
items.hint3: If children are trained well at home, which problems in society become fewer?
items.solution:
Answer: D. helps in reduction of social vices

Responsible parents care for their children, give them moral training and discipline, and watch the company they keep. Children raised this way are less likely to fall into social vices, such as crime, cultism and drug abuse, and a society with fewer vices develops better.

How to tell: the link between the home and the nation is the child's behaviour. Good upbringing produces disciplined citizens, which means fewer social vices.

Why not the others:
A. promotes political participation: this is not the main link between parenting and national development.
B. ensures upbringing of strict leaders: parenting aims at disciplined, responsible children, not strict leaders.
C. emphasizes equality in the society: equality is a principle of democracy and the rule of law, not the main gift of good parenting.

Exam tip: for questions on the importance of the family or parents, look for the option about moral training or fewer social vices.

items.hint1: Traffic regulations apply to everyone who uses the road. Look for the option that is a full definition rather than a part of one.
items.hint2: Driving on express roads is an activity, and 'rules of traffic jam' does not describe any real set of rules.
items.hint3: One remaining option covers only people on foot. Which one covers the rules and good conduct for all road users?
items.solution:
Answer: C. codes and ethics of traffic

Traffic regulations are the rules, codes and standards of good conduct that guide everyone who uses the road: drivers, riders, cyclists and pedestrians. They exist to keep traffic orderly and road users safe.

How to tell: a definition must cover the whole idea. 'Codes and ethics of traffic' covers all road users, even though the wording is loose.

Why not the others:
A. rules of traffic jam: this is not a real set of rules and does not define traffic regulations.
B. rules guiding pedestrians: this is too narrow, because it leaves out drivers and other road users.
D. driving on express roads: this is an activity on the road, not a definition of the rules.

Exam tip: in 'meaning of' questions, reject an option that covers only one group when the term applies to everyone. The widest correct option is usually the definition.

items.hint1: Picture a traffic warden at a busy junction. What are they doing with their hands and whistle?
items.hint2: Making laws and rules is the work of the legislature, not of traffic wardens.
items.hint3: Between putting up road signs and directing moving vehicles, which is the daily work of a traffic warden?
items.solution:
Answer: C. control of traffic flow

Traffic wardens are officers who stand at junctions and busy roads to direct vehicles and pedestrians. Their job is to keep traffic moving in an orderly way and to prevent jams and accidents.

How to tell: the traffic warden's work is on the road, directing movement. That is control of traffic flow.

Why not the others:
A. presentation of traffic legislation: bills and laws are presented and passed in the legislature.
B. mounting of traffic signs: signs are put up by road and works agencies, not by wardens directing traffic.
D. formulation of rules and regulations: making rules is the job of lawmakers and government bodies, not wardens.

Exam tip: for questions on what an official or agency does, match each option to the body that really does it. Lawmaking belongs to the legislature; enforcing and directing belongs to officers on the road.

items.hint1: Recall the ways communities in conflict can settle their differences peacefully, such as talking and using a go-between.
items.hint2: Diligence means hard work, and commendation means praise. Neither settles a quarrel.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one is about changing attitudes and values over time. Which one is a way of settling the dispute itself?
items.solution:
Answer: B. compromise

Compromise is a way of resolving conflict in which each side gives up part of what it wants so that both can reach an agreement. It sits in the list of conflict resolution mechanisms with dialogue, negotiation, mediation and arbitration.

How to tell: a conflict resolution mechanism must be a way of settling a dispute. Of the options, only compromise is on the syllabus list.

Why not the others:
A. reorientation: this means changing attitudes or values, as in value reorientation, not a method of settling a dispute.
C. commendation: this means praising someone, not settling a dispute.
D. diligence: this means working hard and carefully, not settling a dispute.

Exam tip: learn the list of conflict resolution mechanisms: dialogue, negotiation, mediation, arbitration and compromise. If an option is not on that list, it is probably a value or a quality, not a mechanism.

items.hint1: An island stands alone, cut off from everything around it. The saying says people are not like that.
items.hint2: The saying is about people and other people, not about plants and animals or about marriage.
items.hint3: Two options remain. One is about people in general needing each other, and one narrows it to the government. Which matches the saying?
items.solution:
Answer: C. individuals need the cooperation of others to progress

'No man is an island' means no person can live and succeed completely alone. People depend on one another, so cooperation and good relationships are needed for everyone to progress.

How to tell: an island is cut off. Saying a person is not an island means a person is connected to, and depends on, other people.

Why not the others:
A. mankind needs plants and animals: the saying is about people depending on other people.
B. citizens cannot operate without the government: the saying is about people in general, not the government.
D. humans are made to marry: the saying is about cooperation with everyone, not marriage.

Exam tip: for sayings and proverbs, picture the image first, here an island standing alone, then choose the option that matches its general meaning rather than a narrow case.

items.hint1: Notice the word 'cannot'. You are looking for the option that is proper drug use, not abuse.
items.hint2: Drug abuse includes taking too much of a drug and taking drugs without a doctor's approval.
items.hint3: Which option describes a patient following exactly what the doctor ordered?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Consumption of the right dosage of prescribed drugs

Drug use means taking a drug correctly, as a doctor or pharmacist directs. Drug abuse means taking drugs wrongly: too much, for the wrong reason, without authorisation, or dealing in illegal drugs.

How to tell: taking the right dosage of a drug a doctor prescribed is correct use, so it cannot be called drug abuse. The other three are forms of misuse or abuse.

Why not the others:
B. Trafficking of hard substances: dealing in illegal hard drugs is a drug offence, grouped with drug abuse in Civic Education.
C. Consumption of high dosage of legal drugs: taking more than the right dose is abuse, even if the drug is legal.
D. Taking drugs without authorization: using drugs without a prescription or approval is abuse.

Exam tip: in 'not' questions, test each option against the definition and pick the one that fits correct practice. Prescription plus right dosage means proper use.

items.hint1: The question asks about the trafficking act itself, what traffickers do, not what is done to help victims.
items.hint2: Counselling and empowerment are things done to help victims after they are rescued.
items.hint3: Which option is something a trafficker does at the very start, to get hold of a victim?
items.solution:
Answer: D. recruitment of victims

Human trafficking is the buying, selling or moving of people for forced labour, sexual exploitation or other abuse. It happens in stages: recruitment of victims, moving them to another place, and exploiting them.

How to tell: recruitment is the first stage, when traffickers deceive or force victims, often with false promises of jobs or education. It is part of the trafficking act.

Why not the others:
A. liberation of victims: freeing victims is a response to trafficking, not part of it.
B. counseling of victims: counselling helps victims recover and is a response to trafficking.
C. empowerment of victims: empowering victims helps them rebuild their lives and is a response to trafficking.

Exam tip: in trafficking questions, sort each option into what traffickers do (recruit, transport, exploit) or what others do to help (rescue, counsel, rehabilitate, empower).

items.hint1: Think about the purposes for which traffickers move people, and which one is most common for women and girls.
items.hint2: Entrepreneurship and empowerment are good things that help people, not purposes of trafficking.
items.hint3: Of the two exploitative options left, one is a way traffickers control victims and the other is the main purpose for trafficking women. Which is the purpose?
items.solution:
Answer: B. sexual servitude

Human trafficking moves people for purposes such as forced labour, domestic work, organ harvesting and sexual exploitation. For women and girls, textbooks and United Nations reports show that sexual exploitation, including forced prostitution, is the most common purpose.

How to tell: the key word is 'mainly'. Sexual servitude is the main purpose listed for trafficked women.

Why not the others:
A. entrepreneurship: running a business is a positive activity, not a purpose of trafficking.
C. debt bondage: traffickers do use false debts to control victims, but this is a method of control rather than the main purpose for women.
D. empowerment: this helps people, which is the opposite of trafficking.

Exam tip: when an option is something good, such as empowerment or entrepreneurship, it cannot be a purpose of a crime. Remove those first.

items.hint1: Think about which system of the body HIV attacks.
items.hint2: Repletion means being filled up or restored. HIV does not build up any part of the body, so options with 'repletion' do not fit.
items.hint3: Look at the full name of the virus in the question. The middle word is made of two parts. Which option uses both parts?
items.solution:
Answer: B. immune deficiency

HIV attacks and destroys the white blood cells that defend the body against disease, called CD4 cells. As these cells are lost, the immune system becomes weak. This weakness is called immune deficiency, and in its late stage it leads to AIDS, Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome.

How to tell: the name says it. Human Immunodeficiency Virus is the virus that causes immune deficiency, meaning the body's defence system is lacking.

Why not the others:
A. immune repletion: repletion means being filled up, but HIV weakens the immune system.
C. virus deficiency: this is not a real condition; HIV causes a shortage of defence cells, not of viruses.
D. virus repletion: this is not a medical term used for what HIV does to the body.

Exam tip: expand abbreviations in health questions. HIV means Human Immunodeficiency Virus and AIDS means Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, and the words often point to the answer.

items.hint1: Babies usually get HIV from one particular person. Think about who that is.
items.hint2: Babies do not have sex and do not normally share sharp objects, so those routes do not fit.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, which is a route from mother to child that happens every day in a baby's life?
items.solution:
Answer: C. breast feeding

Most babies who have HIV got it from their mothers. This is called mother-to-child transmission, and it can happen during pregnancy, during birth, or through breastfeeding. Of the options given, breastfeeding is the only mother-to-child route.

How to tell: find the route that links a baby to an infected mother. Breast milk can carry the virus, so an infected mother can pass HIV to her baby through breastfeeding. Birth is also a common route, but it is not one of the options.

Why not the others:
A. blood transfusion: a baby can receive blood, but screened blood makes this a rare route, not the common one.
B. sharp object sharing: this is a route for older children and adults, not a common one for babies.
D. sexual transmission: this does not apply to babies.

Exam tip: for HIV transmission questions, match the route to the person in the stem. For babies, choose the mother-to-child route among the options.

items.hint1: Youth empowerment means helping young people become self-reliant, able to earn a living on their own.
items.hint2: Taxes take money away from people, and lobbying is persuading lawmakers. Neither makes a young person self-reliant.
items.hint3: Two options give young people money. One pays for schooling, and one lets them start a business of their own. Which leads straight to self-reliance?
items.solution:
Answer: D. provision of startup capital

Youth empowerment means giving young people the skills, tools and resources to become self-reliant and productive. In the syllabus, a main way of doing this is providing startup capital, meaning money or soft loans to start a business, often after skills training, through agencies such as NDE and SMEDAN.

How to tell: startup capital lets a young person open a trade or business, earn income and even employ others. That is self-reliance, the aim of empowerment.

Why not the others:
A. imposition of taxes: taxes take money away from young people rather than empowering them.
B. political lobbying: this is persuading lawmakers to support a cause, not a way of making youths self-reliant.
C. granting of bursaries: bursaries help students pay for education, which is useful, but textbooks place them under access to education rather than empowerment for self-reliance.

Exam tip: for youth empowerment questions, choose the option that leads most directly to self-reliance, such as skills training, soft loans or startup capital.

items.hint1: The syllabus has its own list of the types of youth empowerment skills. Recall that list, not general words from education books.
items.hint2: The syllabus list includes intellectual, communicative, creative, leadership and life-coping skills. Terms that are not on that list are unlikely to be the answer.
items.hint3: One syllabus skill type covers trades such as tailoring, carpentry and hairdressing, where you work with your hands. Which option is the syllabus name for it?
items.solution:
Answer: C. manipulative skills

The WASSCE syllabus names the types of youth empowerment skills as manipulative, intellectual, communicative, creative or artistic, leadership, life-coping and value skills. Manipulative skills are the practical skills of using the hands and tools, as in tailoring, carpentry, welding and hairdressing, which help young people earn a living.

How to tell: of the four options, only manipulative skills is on the syllabus list of youth empowerment skills.

Why not the others:
A. transversal skills: this is a general education term for skills used across many areas, and it is not on the syllabus list.
B. cross-curricular skills: this is a school curriculum term, not a syllabus youth empowerment skill.
D. non-cognitive skills: this is a general education term, not one of the skill types in the syllabus.

Exam tip: learn the syllabus list of youth empowerment skills by heart. In Civic Education, 'manipulative' means working with the hands, not tricking people.

items.hint1: Notice the word 'not'. Three options are on the list of youth empowerment skills and one is not.
items.hint2: Youth empowerment skills help young people earn a living, work with others and lead. Being able to lead and being able to pass on ideas both fit that list.
items.hint3: Two options are left. Ask which one you have seen named in a syllabus list of youth empowerment skills, and which one you have not.
items.solution:
Answer: D. Investigation skills

Youth empowerment skills are the abilities that help young people become self-reliant and useful citizens. Standard lists include leadership, communication, self-reliance or life-coping, manipulative, intellectual and creative skills.

How to tell: leadership, communication and self-reliance skills are all named in standard lists of youth empowerment skills. Investigation skills is not named as one.

Why not the others:
A. Leadership skills: these are on the list, because they help youths guide and organise others.
B. Communication skills: these are on the list, because they help youths express ideas and work with others.
C. Self-reliance skills: these are on the list, because being able to support oneself is the main aim of youth empowerment.

Exam tip: in 'which is not' skill questions, tick off each option you can find on the syllabus list. The one you cannot find is the answer.

items.hint1: Impeachment is how an official is removed from office for serious misconduct. Think about which arm of government acts as a check on the president.
items.hint2: The president is the head of the executive, so the executive cannot be the arm that removes him or her.
items.hint3: The Supreme Court is part of the judiciary, so those two options stand or fall together. Is the power with the courts or with the lawmakers?
items.solution:
Answer: C. legislature

Impeachment is the process of charging and removing a president or other executive officer for gross misconduct. In Nigeria, the power to impeach the president lies with the legislature, the National Assembly, as a check on the executive.

How to tell: the National Assembly starts the process, votes on it, and makes the final decision to remove the president. The Chief Justice sets up a panel to investigate the charges, but the panel does not remove the president; the legislature does.

Why not the others:
A. executive: the president heads the executive, so it cannot remove its own head by impeachment.
B. judiciary: the courts interpret the law and do not hold the power to remove the president by impeachment.
D. supreme court: it is the highest court, part of the judiciary, and does not impeach the president.

Exam tip: remember the jobs of the three arms: the legislature makes laws and can impeach, the executive carries out laws, and the judiciary interprets laws. Removing a president is a check by the lawmakers on the executive.

items.hint1: In a federal system, the Constitution shares out law-making powers using lists. Recall the names of the lists and who uses each.
items.hint2: 'Joint list' is not a name used in the Nigerian Constitution.
items.hint3: One list is for the federal government alone and one is left to the states. Which list is shared by both?
items.solution:
Answer: C. concurrent list

In Nigeria's federal system, the Constitution divides law-making powers into three lists. The exclusive list is for the federal government alone. The concurrent list covers matters on which both federal and state governments can make laws. Residual matters are those on neither list, and they are left to the states.

How to tell: concurrent means happening together. Matters on which both federal and state governments make laws are on the concurrent list.

Why not the others:
A. residual list: residual matters belong to the states alone.
B. exclusive list: this is for the federal government alone.
D. joint list: this is not a term used in the Nigerian Constitution.

Exam tip: remember the lists by who uses them: exclusive for the federal government, concurrent for federal and state together, residual for the states.

items.hint1: The exclusive list holds matters that concern the whole nation, handled by the federal government alone.
items.hint2: Education and industries are on the concurrent list, so states can make laws on them too.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, roads are built by federal, state and local governments. Which matter would be dangerous to leave to each state on its own?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Defence of the nation

The exclusive list holds matters that affect the whole country and need one national policy, so only the federal government can make laws on them. Defence is on it, along with matters such as foreign affairs, currency and immigration.

How to tell: a country can have only one army protecting its borders. States cannot keep their own armies, so defence is exclusive to the federal government.

Why not the others:
A. Provision of education: education is on the concurrent list, shared by federal and state governments.
C. Provision of good roads: roads are built by all three tiers, with federal, state and local roads.
D. Establishment of industries: industrial development is on the concurrent list.

Exam tip: for exclusive list questions, ask whether the matter must be the same for the whole country. Defence, foreign affairs, currency and citizenship are exclusive; education, health and industry are shared.

items.hint1: Think about what these officials do. Do they make laws, carry them out, or judge cases?
items.hint2: They do not make laws and do not sit in courts.
items.hint3: The civil service is made up of permanent career officials, while these three are political appointees. Which remaining arm carries out government policies?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Executive

The executive is the arm of government that carries out laws and policies. At each level it includes political office holders appointed to head departments: ministers at the federal level, commissioners at the state level, and supervisory councillors at the local government level.

How to tell: all three head departments and carry out policies at their level of government. That is executive work.

Why not the others:
B. Legislature: this is the law-making arm, made up of elected members such as senators and councillors, not ministers or commissioners.
C. Judiciary: this is the arm made up of judges and courts that interpret the law.
D. Civil service: it is made up of permanent career officials, and it is not one of the three organs of government.

Exam tip: match officials to their level: minister (federal), commissioner (state), supervisory councillor (local). All three are executive. Legislators are senators, House members and councillors.

items.hint1: Think about how close each tier of government is to ordinary people in villages and towns.
items.hint2: Local government has nothing to do with promoting foreign culture, and it is not tied to consensus politics.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one is a system where power sits in one central government. Which one describes government brought close to the people?
items.solution:
Answer: C. grassroot government

Local government is the tier of government closest to the people. It brings government to the grassroots, meaning the local community level, so people can take part in decisions and receive services such as markets, primary health care and local roads.

How to tell: 'grassroot' means the ordinary people at the local level. Local government exists to govern at that level.

Why not the others:
A. unitary government: this is a system where power is held by one central government, and local government exists under both unitary and federal systems.
B. consensus politics: this means reaching decisions by general agreement, not the purpose of local government.
D. foreign culture: local government is about local communities, not foreign culture.

Exam tip: when a question asks what local government does or supports, look for words about the local people: grassroots, closeness, participation and basic local services.

items.hint1: Think about what makes a government representative: who chooses the people in power, and how the people keep control over them.
items.hint2: In a representative government the people rule through representatives they choose, so an option that keeps power in a few hands or in one centre goes against the idea.
items.hint3: Of the options left, one is about how regions work together and one is about how the people pick their leaders. Which belongs to representation?
items.solution:
Answer: D. periodic elections

In a representative government, the people do not make laws themselves. They choose representatives to do it for them, and they must be able to renew or withdraw that choice. Elections held at regular intervals, for example every four years in Nigeria, are how they do this.

How to tell: ask how the people control their representatives. Regular elections are the option that gives them that control, because a representative who fails can be voted out.

Why not the others:
A. minority rule: representative government rests on majority rule, where the choice of most voters decides.
B. inter-regional cooperation: regions can cooperate under many systems of government, so it is not a feature of representation.
C. centralization of power: this describes where power sits, not how the people choose who holds it, and power gathered in few hands works against government by the people.

Exam tip: for a feature of a type of democracy, look for the option that shows the people choosing or controlling their rulers, such as periodic elections, majority rule or popular sovereignty.

items.hint1: The word direct is the key. Ask who takes part in government personally, rather than through someone else.
items.hint2: When citizens send representatives to act for them, that is indirect, or representative, democracy, which is the opposite of direct democracy.
items.hint3: Among the options left, which one describes the citizens as a whole rather than a smaller group of them?
items.solution:
Answer: D. all the citizens

Direct democracy means the citizens themselves meet and decide on laws and policies, with no representatives in between. In the textbook definition, every citizen has the right to take part.

How to tell: direct means no one stands between the people and the decision, so the decision-makers are the citizens as a whole.

Why not the others:
A. only male citizens: limiting it to one sex is not part of the definition. In ancient Athens, the usual example, only adult men counted as citizens, but that was a limit on who was a citizen, not the meaning of direct democracy.
B. only adult male citizens: for the same reason, this describes who Athens allowed, not what direct democracy means.
C. citizens representatives: government through representatives is indirect, or representative, democracy.

Exam tip: match the type of democracy to its key word. Direct means the people decide by themselves. Indirect or representative means they choose others to decide for them.

items.hint1: Individual freedom in politics includes the freedom to choose, to join groups and to oppose the government peacefully. Ask which option gives citizens the most choice.
items.hint2: A system where one ruler holds power, or where only one party is allowed, leaves citizens few lawful ways to disagree.
items.hint3: Of the options left, one is about political parties and one is about community life. Which one gives citizens a real choice at elections?
items.solution:
Answer: B. multi-party system

In a multi-party system, many political parties can be formed and compete for power. Citizens are free to join the party they like, to vote for different programmes, and to oppose the government through another party. That freedom of choice is a large part of individual political freedom.

How to tell: the more choices citizens have without fear, the more freedom they enjoy. Only B widens their choices.

Why not the others:
A. one party system: only one party is allowed, so citizens cannot choose between parties or form a legal opposition.
C. autocratic system: one ruler or a small group holds power without the consent of the people, which limits freedom.
D. communal system: this describes shared community life and ownership, not a way of organising political choice.

Exam tip: when a question links freedom or democracy to a party system, pick the system that gives the most choice. One-party and autocratic options usually mean less freedom.

items.hint1: Before looking at the pairs, sort the seven terms into two groups: things a society needs, and problems it would be better off without.
items.hint2: The absence of a social problem is good news. Political apathy is one such problem, so a pair that contains it cannot spell doom.
items.hint3: Now make the same check for human trafficking and HIV/AIDS. You are looking for the pair in which both items are things a society cannot do without.
items.solution:
Answer: D. II and VII

Law and order keeps life and property safe, and fundamental human rights protect every person from abuse. Without law and order, a society slides into disorder. Without rights, people are open to oppression. That is why losing both would be ruinous.

How to tell: sort the list first.
Things a society needs: II. Law and order, V. Popular participation, VI. Responsible parenting, VII. Fundamental Human Rights.
Social problems: I. Political apathy, III. Human trafficking, IV. HIV/AIDS.
The absence of a problem is good news, so only a pair made of two needs can spell doom. D is the only such pair among the options.

Why not the others:
A. I and II: political apathy is a problem, so its absence would help society.
B. IV and V: HIV/AIDS is a problem, so its absence would be a blessing.
C. III and VI: human trafficking is a problem, so its absence would be good.

Exam tip: with a numbered list of terms, sort the items into good and bad before reading the pairs. The wording of the stem, such as absence, presence, threat or benefit, tells you which group to pick from.

items.hint1: An entitlement is something a person is owed. Ask which items on the list belong to a child personally.
items.hint2: Popular participation, such as voting and contesting elections, is an activity of adult citizens, not something owed to a child.
items.hint3: Of the pairs left, compare the item they do not share. Is it owed to the child personally, or is it a condition of the whole society?
items.solution:
Answer: C. VI and VII

An entitlement is something a person is owed. Every child is owed care, protection and upbringing by responsible parents, and every child holds fundamental human rights, such as the right to life and to dignity. In Nigeria, the Child Rights Act of 2003 sets out both as the child's due.

How to tell: ask of each item, is this owed to the child personally? Responsible parenting (VI) and fundamental human rights (VII) pass. Law and order (II) is a condition of the whole society, and popular participation (V) is an activity of adult citizens.

Why not the others:
A. II and V: neither is owed to the child personally. Law and order serves the whole society, and popular participation, such as voting, belongs to adults.
B. V and VII: VII fits, but popular participation is not a child's entitlement, since voting in Nigeria starts at 18.
D. II and VI: VI fits, but law and order is a condition of the whole society, not something a child holds.

Exam tip: for entitlement or right questions, pick the items owed to the person named in the stem. Leave out duties they perform and conditions that belong to society as a whole.

items.hint1: Think about the difference between lawful and unlawful ways of dealing with a bad government.
items.hint2: Violence against officials, or an uprising against the government, breaks the law and can cause more harm than the bad governance itself.
items.hint3: Of the two lawful options left, which one can actually correct or remove a bad leader, rather than only complain about them?
items.solution:
Answer: D. recourse to constitutional means

The constitution gives citizens lawful ways to hold leaders to account: voting them out at the next election, going to court, pressing legislators to impeach, or recalling a legislator. These tools can correct or remove a bad government without breaking the law or the peace.

How to tell: best means both lawful and effective. Constitutional means are the option that is both.

Why not the others:
A. criticism of government officials: it is lawful and useful, but on its own it cannot remove or correct a government.
B. attacks on government officials: violence is a crime and does not fix governance.
C. revolt against such governments: an uprising is unconstitutional and can lead to bloodshed and disorder.

Exam tip: when asked for the best way to check leaders or defend rights, choose the lawful, constitutional option over violent or merely verbal ones.

items.hint1: The stem asks how to stop one part of government from getting in the way of another. Think about how the three arms of government relate to each other.
items.hint2: Giving traditional rulers more roles does nothing about how the arms of government relate, and joining government functions together makes overlap easier, not harder.
items.hint3: Two ideas are left. One keeps each arm to its own work. The other lets each arm watch and limit the others. Which one is aimed at avoiding interference?
items.solution:
Answer: B. clear-cut separation of governmental powers

Separation of powers divides government into three arms: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets them. In Civic Education texts, its stated purpose is that each arm does its own work without interference from the others.

How to tell: the aim in the stem is to avoid undue interference. Keeping each arm clearly within its own duties is the principle built for that aim.

Why not the others:
A. more roles for traditional rulers: traditional rulers are not one of the three arms, so this does nothing about interference between them.
C. proper fusion of government functions: fusion joins the arms together, as in a parliamentary system where ministers sit in the legislature, which makes overlap more likely.
D. checks and balances: it lets each arm watch and limit the others, for example the legislature impeaching the president, so it is controlled interference to prevent abuse of power, not the avoidance of interference.

Exam tip: separation of powers answers questions about keeping the arms apart and preventing interference. Checks and balances answers questions about preventing abuse of power by letting one arm control another.

items.hint1: Immunity means being protected from something. Ask what the constitution protects certain office holders from.
items.hint2: The power to forgive a convicted person is a different constitutional power, called the prerogative of mercy.
items.hint3: Of the options left, which one describes protection from court cases, and which ones describe something much wider?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Some public officers cannot be sued

The immunity clause, Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, protects the President, Vice-President, Governors and Deputy Governors from civil or criminal cases in court while they are in office. They can be taken to court after they leave office.

How to tell: immunity protects a named few from court action. Some officers and cannot be sued match that.

Why not the others:
B. The president can grant pardon to any prisoner/criminal: this is the prerogative of mercy, a separate power.
C. Public officers are not accountable to the electorate: these officers can still be voted out or impeached, so they remain accountable.
D. There is absence of arbitrary rule: immunity is taught as a limit on the rule of law, so it can make arbitrary rule easier, not remove it.

Exam tip: for immunity questions, remember three facts: who (the President, Vice-President, Governors and Deputy Governors), what (no court cases against them), and when (only while in office).

items.hint1: Neutral means not taking sides. Ask which sides a civil servant might be tempted to take.
items.hint2: Security of tenure is a separate feature of the civil service. It is about keeping one's job, not about taking sides.
items.hint3: Of the options left, which one is about the civil servant's own political loyalty, and which are about how civil servants are hired?
items.solution:
Answer: D. not be affiliated to any political party

Civil servants serve whichever government is in power, and governments change after elections. To serve each one loyally, they must not take sides in party politics. In the civil service rules taught in the syllabus, this means they do not join or work for a political party while in service.

How to tell: neutrality is about taking no sides, and the sides in government are political parties.

Why not the others:
A. be appointed by a neutral body: this is about how they are hired, not about their own conduct once in office.
B. be recruited on the basis of federal character: this is about sharing jobs fairly among the states, not about political sides.
C. have security of tenure: this is about keeping their job, a separate feature.

Exam tip: learn each civil service feature by its one key idea. Neutrality means no party politics. Anonymity means no personal credit or blame. Permanence and security of tenure mean the job stays when governments change.

items.hint1: Political apathy means lack of interest in politics. Look for the signs of someone pulling away from political life.
items.hint2: In an except question, three options fit the definition. Test each one: does it show a citizen holding back from politics?
items.hint3: Check each option: does it describe someone staying away from politics, or someone deeply involved in it?
items.solution:
Answer: B. rigging of elections

Political apathy is a lack of interest in politics, shown by staying away from political activities. Rigging is the opposite: it is done by people keen to win power, and it is electoral malpractice, a crime. In the syllabus, rigging is listed as a cause of apathy, because it makes voters feel their votes do not count, but it is not a form of it.

How to tell: in an except question, find the odd one out. Three options show citizens holding back. One shows active wrongdoing.

Why not the others:
A. refusal to register for voting: a citizen who will not register is staying out of politics, a form of apathy.
C. lack of interest: this is the meaning of apathy itself.
D. refusal to give information: refusing to give information to the authorities is listed as a form of apathy.

Exam tip: for except questions, test each option against the definition. Apathy means holding back, so an option that shows active involvement, lawful or not, is the odd one out.

items.hint1: Think about what any organisation does when it has less money than it planned for.
items.hint2: Contesting elections is the work of political parties, not civil society organisations, and starting debates is a normal function of CSOs rather than a result of lacking money.
items.hint3: Two options are left. One keeps the CSO independent. The other makes it depend on the government it is meant to watch. Which is the direct result of a shortage of money?
items.solution:
Answer: C. scale back activities

Civil society organisations get money from members, donors and grants. When funding is inadequate, they cannot pay for all their programmes, so they are forced to reduce them. The syllabus lists inadequate funding among the problems of civil society for this reason.

How to tell: the stem asks what the shortage may force a CSO to do. Doing less is the direct result of having less money.

Why not the others:
A. lobby for funds from the government: CSOs are meant to watch and check government, so depending on it for money would weaken their independence. It is not the effect taught.
B. contest for political power: CSOs are non-partisan and do not seek power. That is what political parties do.
D. stimulate debate and discussion: this is a normal function of CSOs, not a result of lack of money.

Exam tip: for questions on the effect of a problem, choose the option that follows directly from the problem. Options that are normal functions, or that go against the body's nature, are distractors.

items.hint1: The stem is about poverty. Look for the option that improves people's own ability to earn a living.
items.hint2: Criticising rigging is about free and fair elections, not about poverty.
items.hint3: Of the options left, which one works directly on people, and which ones work on government or lawmakers?
items.solution:
Answer: B. promoting youth empowerment

Poverty falls when people gain skills, jobs or money to start a business. Many CSOs run skills training, vocational programmes and small loans for young people, which help them earn a living. That is a direct way of helping government reduce poverty.

How to tell: match the option to the problem in the stem. Poverty is about earning, and B is the option that acts directly on people's ability to earn.

Why not the others:
A. influencing government decisions: this is advocacy, which can shape policy but does not by itself reduce poverty.
C. criticizing electoral malpractice: this is about free and fair elections, not poverty.
D. exerting influence on legislation: this is also advocacy, aimed at lawmakers rather than at the poor.

Exam tip: when a question links a body to a specific problem, pick the option that acts on that problem directly. General advocacy options are usually distractors.

items.hint1: The question asks what CSOs are not known for. Recall the key difference between civil society and political parties.
items.hint2: CSOs are commonly praised for defending democracy and watching over government, so options describing those roles fit them.
items.hint3: Of the options left, which one would turn a CSO into a body that seeks power?
items.solution:
Answer: A. establishing new political parties

Civil society organisations are non-partisan: they speak for citizens and check government, but they do not seek to form a government. Forming a party to contest elections is the work of politicians, so it is not a characteristic of CSOs.

How to tell: three options are well-known CSO roles. One is the work of political parties.

Why not the others:
B. advocating for benefits of democracy: CSOs promote democracy and good governance.
C. checkmating the excesses of government: checking abuse of power is a main role of CSOs.
D. acting as training ground for future leaders: members learn leadership in CSOs, and some later go into public life.

Exam tip: remember the dividing line. Political parties seek power, while CSOs and pressure groups seek to influence those in power. An option about forming parties or contesting elections does not describe a CSO.

items.hint1: Think about how workers, through their unions, press their employer for better pay or conditions.
items.hint2: Police action is used by government, not by workers, and quitting the job ends the worker's claim instead of pressing it.
items.hint3: Of the two protests left, which is organised by trade unions and recognised in labour law, and which is a rare personal act?
items.solution:
Answer: C. industrial strike

An industrial strike is when workers, usually through their trade union, stop work together to press their demands, such as better pay or conditions. It is the recognised way public servants protest. In Nigeria, unions such as the NLC and ASUU use it, and labour law sets rules for it.

How to tell: established means recognised and commonly used. The industrial strike is the standard, union-organised protest of workers.

Why not the others:
A. police action: the police are used by government to keep order, not by workers to protest.
B. hunger strike: refusing food is a rare personal protest, not the established method of public servants.
D. mass resignation: quitting ends the job, so the workers lose the very interests they want to protect.

Exam tip: for questions on how workers or unions protect their interests, the expected answer is usually a collective, lawful action such as a strike, negotiation or collective bargaining.

items.hint1: Anonymous means without a name. Ask what civil servants stay nameless about in their official work.
items.hint2: Being fair in judgement is the feature called impartiality, and civil servants are not required to stay away from voting.
items.hint3: Two options are left. One is about who receives the credit or blame for government work, the other about being known in politics. Which matches the textbook meaning of anonymity?
items.solution:
Answer: A. not expected to take credit or blame in their duty

Civil servants advise ministers and carry out policy behind the scenes. Under the feature called anonymity, the public is not told which official did what, so the credit or blame for a policy goes to the minister or political head, not to the civil servant.

How to tell: link anonymous to without a name. A civil servant's name is not attached to the work, so they are not credited or blamed for it.

Why not the others:
B. expected to abstain from voting during elections: civil servants can vote like other citizens. They only stay out of party politics.
C. expected to be fair and impartial in judgement: this is impartiality.
D. not expected to be politically known in the society: this is close, but anonymity is about who takes credit or blame for official work, not about fame. Staying out of politics is neutrality.

Exam tip: anonymity questions are about credit and blame. If an option says who takes the praise or the blame for government work, that points to anonymity.
